title: SVM III — The Kernel Trick

blocks.t: From the notes
The kernel trick, as written

When the data is not linearly separable, we convert it into
higher dimensions where it becomes linearly separable.

Example: 1D points $-3,-2,-1,1,2,3$ with the middle ones in one class —
no single point separates them. Add $x^2$ as a second dimension and now a
line does.

But going to higher dimensions is costly. So we use the
kernel trick: we do not actually transform the data, we only
compute the dot product as if we had.

Kernels: linear, polynomial, RBF (radial basis
function, the most used one), sigmoid.

blocks.cap:
Concentric circles. In 2D no line works. Lift with
$z=x_1^2+x_2^2$ and a flat plane separates them perfectly. Projected back, that
plane is a circle — and an RBF SVM finds exactly this boundary without ever
constructing $z$.

blocks.t: Why the trick is possible
Recall the soft-margin dual from Topic 73:

\max_{\alpha} \sum_i \alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_i\sum_j \alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j
 \boxed{\langle x_i,x_j\rangle},
\qquad 0\le\alpha_i\le C, \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0,
and the prediction rule, obtained by substituting $w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i$:
f(x)=\sum_{i\in SV}\alpha_i y_i \boxed{\langle x_i,x\rangle} + b .

The raw feature vectors never appear on their own — only inside
inner products. So if we want to work in a transformed space $\phi(x)$, every
occurrence becomes $\langle \phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle$. If some function $K$
satisfies
K(x_i,x_j) = \langle \phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle

and is cheap to evaluate, we can compute the entire model without ever
constructing $\phi$. That is the kernel trick.

Mercer's condition. A symmetric function $K$ is a valid kernel exactly
when its Gram matrix $K_{ij}=K(x_i,x_j)$ is positive semi-definite for every
finite sample. PSD-ness is what guarantees some $\phi$ exists and keeps the dual
convex. Kernels are closed under addition, multiplication by a positive scalar,
products, and composition with a positive power series — which is how new
kernels are built.
The polynomial kernel, expanded by hand
Take $d=2$ features and the kernel $K(x,z)=(x^Tz+1)^2$. Expand it:

\begin{aligned}
(x_1z_1+x_2z_2+1)^2
&= x_1^2z_1^2 + x_2^2z_2^2 + 2x_1x_2z_1z_2 + 2x_1z_1 + 2x_2z_2 + 1
[3pt]
&= \big\langle
(x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt2 x_1x_2, \sqrt2 x_1, \sqrt2 x_2, 1), 
(z_1^2, z_2^2, \sqrt2 z_1z_2, \sqrt2 z_1, \sqrt2 z_2, 1)
\big\rangle .
\end{aligned}
So $\phi(x)=(x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2 x_1x_2,\sqrt2 x_1,\sqrt2 x_2,1)\in\mathbb{R}^6$.

Computing $\phi$ explicitly costs 6 multiplications per point plus a
6-dimensional dot product. Computing $K$ costs one 2-dimensional dot product
plus an add and a square. The gap explodes with dimension: for general $d$ and
degree $p$ the feature space has $\binom{d+p}{p}$ coordinates — for $d=100$,
$p=5$ that is about 96 million features — while $K$ still costs
$O(d)$.
The kernel zoo

head: Kernel
$K(x,z)$
Character
rows: No lift. Use when $d \gg n$ (text, genomics) or when the boundary really is linear. Fastest, interpretable ($w$ exists).
Explicit finite lift of degree $p$; captures feature interactions. Numerically touchy for $p>5$; needs coef0 $>0$ to include lower-order terms.
Infinite-dimensional lift. Local, smooth, universal. The default.
Neural-network flavoured; not PSD for all parameters, so it can misbehave. Rarely the best choice.

blocks.cap:
Two moons, five kernels, identical $C$. The kernel does not tune the
fit — it decides what shape of boundary is expressible at all.

blocks.t: Why RBF is infinite-dimensional
Expand the Gaussian kernel for scalars, with $\gamma=\frac{1}{2}$:

The series never terminates, and the $k$-th term is (a multiple of) a
polynomial kernel of degree $k$. So the RBF kernel is a weighted sum of
polynomial kernels of every degree — its feature map lives in an
infinite-dimensional space. You could never build $\phi(x)$; you can always
evaluate $K$ in $O(d)$.

This is why the RBF SVM is a universal approximator: with enough data
and suitable $\gamma$ it can approximate any continuous decision boundary.
$\gamma$ and $C$: the two dials

blocks.cap:
Eight RBF models. Across: $\gamma$ from 0.1 to 100. Down: $C$ = 0.1
then 100. At $\gamma=100$ the model builds an island around each training
point — memorisation.

blocks.t: Reading $\gamma$

$\gamma$ sets how far the influence of one training point reaches.
Since $K=\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$, the similarity falls to $e^{-1}$ at distance
$1/\sqrt{\gamma}$, so $1/\sqrt\gamma$ is a length scale in feature units.

Small $\gamma$ — wide reach, every point influences the whole space,
the boundary is nearly linear. Underfits.

Large $\gamma$ — each point influences only its immediate
neighbourhood, and the model surrounds individual training points with little
islands. Overfits; in the limit it becomes a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier.

gamma="scale" (the default) sets
$\gamma = \frac{1}{d\cdot\operatorname{Var}(X)}$, which is scale-aware and a
genuinely good starting point — but only if you have scaled your features.

$\gamma$ and $C$ must be tuned together, on a joint log grid. They are
not independent: a large $\gamma$ makes the model flexible enough that even a
small $C$ can overfit, and a small $\gamma$ can be partially compensated by a
large $C$. Tuning $C$ with $\gamma$ fixed, then $\gamma$ with $C$ fixed, walks
into a saddle and misses the good region. Use
GridSearchCV over
np.logspace(-3,3,7) $\times$ np.logspace(-4,2,7).

blocks.t: The cost

The Gram matrix is $n\times n$. At 100{,}000 rows that is $10^{10}$
entries — 80 GB in float64. SVC does not materialise it fully
(cache_size holds a working subset), but training is still between
$O(n^2 d)$ and $O(n^3)$ and becomes impractical past roughly 20{,}000–50{,}000
rows.

Prediction is also not free: $f(x)=\sum_{i\in SV}\alpha_iy_iK(x_i,x)+b$ costs
$O(|SV| \cdot d)$ per query, and $|SV|$ typically grows linearly with $n$. A
kernel SVM trained on a lot of noisy data becomes a slow, memory-hungry model
at serving time — unlike the linear case, where everything collapses into a
single $w$.

The escape hatch: explicit kernel approximation. Nystroem and
RBFSampler (random Fourier features) build a finite $\hat\phi(x)\in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ with $\langle\hat\phi(x),\hat\phi(z)\rangle\approx K(x,z)$, for
$m$ in the hundreds. Feed that into LinearSVC or
SGDClassifier and you get near-RBF accuracy at linear cost, scaling to
millions of rows.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles, make_moons, make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import Nystroem, RBFSampler
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier

# ==================================================================
# 1. PROVING THE TRICK -- explicit lift vs kernel, same answer
# ==================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(6, 2))

def phi(x):                       # feature map for K(x,z) = (x.z + 1)^2
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0], x[:, 1]
    return np.column_stack([x1**2, x2**2, np.sqrt(2)*x1*x2,
                            np.sqrt(2)*x1, np.sqrt(2)*x2, np.ones_like(x1)])

K_explicit = phi(X) @ phi(X).T            # lift, THEN dot product  (6-D)
K_trick    = (X @ X.T + 1) ** 2           # dot product in 2-D, then square
print("identical:", np.allclose(K_explicit, K_trick))   # True
print("dims: explicit 6, kernel 2 -- and this gap explodes with degree")

# For d=100 features at degree 5 the explicit space has
print("features at d=100, p=5:", int(np.math.comb(100 + 5, 5)))   # ~96 million

# ==================================================================
# 2. CIRCLES: linear fails, RBF succeeds
# ==================================================================
Xc, yc = make_circles(600, factor=0.42, noise=0.09, random_state=0)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
for kern in ("linear", "rbf"):
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel=kern, C=1)).fit(Xa, ya)
    print(f"{kern:7s} test acc {m.score(Xb, yb):.4f}")
# linear ~0.50 (chance), rbf ~0.99 -- the boundary is a circle.

# The manual lift gives the same result, at the cost of building the feature:
Xlift_a = np.column_stack([Xa, (Xa**2).sum(1)])
Xlift_b = np.column_stack([Xb, (Xb**2).sum(1)])
print("manual lift + linear SVM:",
      round(SVC(kernel="linear", C=1).fit(Xlift_a, ya).score(Xlift_b, yb), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. TUNING gamma AND C JOINTLY -- never one at a time
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=15, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.05, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("svm", SVC(kernel="rbf"))])
grid = {"svm__C":     np.logspace(-2, 3, 6),
        "svm__gamma": np.logspace(-4, 1, 6)}
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# The heatmap of the joint grid is what you should always look at:
sc = gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].reshape(len(grid["svm__C"]), -1)
print(np.round(sc, 3))

# ==================================================================
# 4. A CUSTOM KERNEL -- any PSD function works
# ==================================================================
def my_rbf(A, B, gamma=0.5):
    # ||a-b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b   (avoids a python loop)
    sq = (A**2).sum(1)[:, None] + (B**2).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * A @ B.T
    return np.exp(-gamma * np.maximum(sq, 0))

custom = SVC(kernel=my_rbf).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)
print("custom kernel works:", round(custom.score(
      StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte), yte), 4))

# You can also precompute the Gram matrix yourself -- useful for kernels over
# non-vector objects (strings, graphs, sets), where there are no "features".
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr)
Gtr = my_rbf(Xs, Xs)
pre = SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(Gtr, ytr)
Xts = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte)
print("precomputed:", round(pre.score(my_rbf(Xts, Xs), yte), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHAT THE MODEL STORES  -- there is no w in kernel space
# ==================================================================
m = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1, gamma="scale").fit(Xs, ytr)
print("support vectors:", m.support_vectors_.shape)   # the model IS these points
try:
    m.coef_
except AttributeError as e:
    print("no coef_ for a nonlinear kernel:", type(e).__name__)
# Prediction: f(x) = sum_i alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b, over support vectors only
manual = (m.dual_coef_ @ my_rbf(m.support_vectors_, Xts[:5],
          gamma=1/(Xs.shape[1]*Xs.var()))).ravel() + m.intercept_
print("decision_function:", m.decision_function(Xts[:5]).round(3))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING UP -- approximate the kernel, then use a linear model
# ==================================================================
Xbig, ybig = make_classification(n_samples=200000, n_features=20,
                                 n_informative=10, random_state=0)
fast = make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        Nystroem(kernel="rbf", gamma=0.05, n_components=400, random_state=0),
        SGDClassifier(loss="hinge", alpha=1e-5, max_iter=30, tol=1e-3))
fast.fit(Xbig[:150000], ybig[:150000])
print("Nystroem + linear SVM on 150k rows:",
      round(fast.score(Xbig[150000:], ybig[150000:]), 4))
# RBFSampler (random Fourier features) is the cheaper, slightly weaker sibling.
Everything on one page
Summary

The trick: the SVM dual and its prediction rule contain the data
only as inner products. Replace $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$ with
$K(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle$ and you train in a
high-dimensional space you never construct.
Valid kernels are exactly those with a PSD Gram matrix (Mercer).

Polynomial $(\gamma x^Tz+r)^p$ — a finite lift to
$\binom{d+p}{p}$ dimensions, computed in $O(d)$.
RBF $\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$ — an infinite lift (expand the
exponential), universal, the default.

$\gamma$ = reach of one point; $1/\sqrt\gamma$ is its length scale.
Small $\gamma$ underfits towards linear, large $\gamma$ overfits towards
1-NN. Tune $\gamma$ and $C$ jointly on a log grid.

Scale features first — both $\gamma$ and the margin are measured in
feature units.

Cost: $O(n^2)$–$O(n^3)$ training, $O(|SV|d)$ per prediction. Beyond
$\sim$20k rows use Nystroem/RBFSampler + a linear model.

No coef_ for a nonlinear kernel — $w$ lives in a space you
never built. The model is the support vectors and their $\alpha_i$.
Interview corner
Q. Explain the kernel trick.

The SVM dual depends on the data only through inner products. A kernel
$K(x,z)$ computes the inner product of two points after a feature map
$\phi$, without ever evaluating $\phi$. So we get the expressiveness of a
high- or infinite-dimensional space at the computational cost of the original
one.
Q. What makes a function a valid kernel?

Symmetry plus positive semi-definiteness of the Gram matrix for every finite
sample (Mercer's condition). That guarantees an implicit $\phi$ exists and the
dual stays convex.
Q. Why is the RBF kernel infinite-dimensional?

Factor $e^{-\frac12\|x-z\|^2}$ into $e^{-\|x\|^2/2}e^{-\|z\|^2/2}e^{x^Tz}$ and
Taylor-expand $e^{x^Tz}=\sum_k (x^Tz)^k/k!$. Every polynomial degree appears
with a positive weight, so the feature space has infinitely many coordinates.
Q. What does $\gamma$ do?

It sets the width of the Gaussian, i.e. how far a single training point's
influence extends. Large $\gamma$ = narrow influence = wiggly boundary and
overfitting (approaching 1-NN); small $\gamma$ = broad influence = nearly
linear boundary and underfitting.
Q. How do $\gamma$ and $C$ interact?

Both increase effective capacity, so they must be tuned jointly. Large $\gamma$
plus large $C$ memorises the training set; small $\gamma$ plus small $C$
underfits badly. The good region is a diagonal band in the $(\log C,\log\gamma)$
plane, which a joint grid search finds and a sequential search does not.
Q. Which kernel would you start with?

Linear if $d \gg n$ (text, genomics) or if you need interpretable coefficients
— it is also far faster. Otherwise RBF, which subsumes the polynomial family
and needs only two hyperparameters. Polynomial when you specifically want
bounded-degree feature interactions; sigmoid essentially never.
Q. Can you get $w$ from a kernel SVM?

Not explicitly, unless the kernel is linear — $w$ lives in the implicit
feature space, which may be infinite-dimensional. The model is stored as the
support vectors, their dual coefficients $\alpha_iy_i$, and $b$; prediction is
$f(x)=\sum_{i\in SV}\alpha_iy_iK(x_i,x)+b$.
Q. Where else does the kernel trick appear?

Kernel PCA, kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes (the covariance
function is a kernel), spectral clustering, and one-class SVM for
anomaly detection. Any algorithm expressible purely in inner products can be
kernelised.
Q. Kernel SVM or gradient boosting on tabular data?

Boosting, almost always: it handles mixed types and missing values, scales to
large $n$, and needs no scaling. Kernel SVMs remain competitive on small,
dense, well-scaled numeric data — especially when $d>n$ — and on structured
inputs where a bespoke kernel encodes real domain knowledge.
Worked Examples
Verifying the kernel trick numerically
Degree-2 polynomial kernel $k(x,z) = (x\cdot z)^2$ corresponds to the explicit map $\varphi(x) = (x_1^2,\;\sqrt2\,x_1x_2,\;x_2^2)$.
Route 1 – kernel, never leaving the original space.
x\cdot z = 1\cdot 3 + 2\cdot 1 = 5, \qquad k(x,z) = 5^2 = 25
Route 2 – explicit feature map.
\varphi(x) = (1, 2\sqrt2, 4), \qquad \varphi(z) = (9, 3\sqrt2, 1)
\varphi(x)\cdot\varphi(z) = 9 + (2\sqrt2)(3\sqrt2) + 4 = 9 + 12 + 4 = 25
Both routes give $25$. The SVM only ever needs dot products, so it can work in the 3-dimensional (or infinite-dimensional, for RBF) space while computing only $k$.

Why RBF is infinite-dimensional. $k(x,z) = \exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$ expands into a power series whose terms correspond to polynomials of every degree, so no finite $\varphi$ exists. The kernel is still computed in one line.
